teaching.h: Why Mandarin grammar feels different from the start
teaching.p: Mandarin has no verb conjugation at all — no tenses, no subject agreement. Instead, meaning comes almost entirely from word order and extra marker words. This is actually good news: once you learn the order, you don't have to memorize dozens of verb forms.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ hē chá — I drink tea

teaching.h: The same verb, for everyone, every time
teaching.p: 喝 (hē, 'drink') never changes, whether it's me, you, or them, past or present. Compare that to English's drink/drinks/drank — Mandarin skips all of that.
teaching.exTranslation: tā hē chá — he drinks tea

teaching.h: Time words go right after the subject
teaching.p: Since verbs can't show tense themselves, Mandarin puts a time word early in the sentence to establish when something happens — and that time word then applies for the rest of the sentence.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ jīntiān hē chá — I today drink tea (I'm drinking tea today)

teaching.h: No plural forms either
teaching.p: Nouns and verbs stay exactly the same whether you mean one or many — quantity gets shown separately, with numbers and measure words (which is exactly what Lesson 2 covers).
teaching.exTranslation: yí gè rén / liǎng gè rén — one person / two people

quiz.q: How does Mandarin show verb tense?
Where do time words usually go?

teaching.h: A concept English simply doesn't have
teaching.p: In Mandarin, you can't just say 'three apples' — a measure word has to sit between the number and the noun, chosen based on the noun's shape or category. English has a faint echo of this ('two pieces of paper'), but Mandarin requires it for almost every noun.
teaching.exTranslation: yí gè rén — one person

teaching.h: 个 (gè) — your safe default
teaching.p: When you're not sure which measure word to use, gè is the closest thing to a universal fallback for people and many general objects — not always technically correct, but usually understood.
teaching.exTranslation: sān gè píngguǒ — three apples

teaching.h: 本 (běn) — specifically for bound objects
teaching.p: Books, magazines, anything with pages bound together.
teaching.exTranslation: liǎng běn shū — two books

teaching.h: 杯 (bēi) — measured by the cup
teaching.p: This measure word doubles as the actual container word too — same pattern as English 'a cup of tea'.
teaching.exTranslation: yì bēi chá — one cup of tea

teaching.h: Common measure words at a glance
teaching.p: These five cover a huge share of daily conversation. When in doubt and none of these obviously fit, 个 (gè) is still the safest fallback.

table.caption: Frequently used measure words
rows: 一杯茶 — a cup of tea
三张纸 — three sheets of paper

quiz.q: Which measure word is for books?

units.title: Key Particles: 了 的 吗

teaching.h: Small words carrying big grammatical jobs
teaching.p: These three particles don't translate word-for-word into English — they're pure grammar markers, each doing a specific job that English handles completely differently (through tense, possessive 's, or a question mark).

teaching.h: 了 (le) — marks that something happened or changed
teaching.p: This is Mandarin's substitute for a past-tense verb ending — instead of changing the verb, you add 了 after it.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ chī le — I ate

teaching.h: 的 (de) — shows possession, like English's 's
teaching.p: Sits between the owner and the thing owned.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ de shū — my book

teaching.h: 吗 (ma) — turns any statement into a yes/no question
teaching.p: The easiest question-forming trick in Mandarin: just add 吗 to the end of a normal sentence, no word order change needed.
teaching.exTranslation: nǐ hē chá ma? — Do you drink tea?

options: at the end of a sentence
quiz.answer: at the end of a sentence

teaching.h: Four different ways to ask, each with its own flavor
teaching.p: Mandarin doesn't have just one question pattern — knowing which to use makes you sound much more natural, not just grammatically correct.

teaching.h: 吗 for a simple yes/no
teaching.p: The one you already know from Lesson 3.
teaching.exTranslation: nǐ shì xuéshēng ma? — Are you a student?

teaching.h: 还是 for choosing between options
teaching.p: When you're offering someone a choice, not just a yes/no.
teaching.exTranslation: nǐ yào chá háishì kāfēi? — Do you want tea or coffee?

teaching.h: Question words stay exactly where the answer would go
teaching.p: This is different from English, where 'what' jumps to the front. In Mandarin, 什么 (what) sits right where the answer word would naturally be.
teaching.exTranslation: nǐ yào shénme? — What do you want?

teaching.h: A-not-A — repeating the verb for a yes/no question
teaching.p: Say the verb, then 不 (not), then the verb again — a very common, casual way to ask yes/no questions.
teaching.exTranslation: nǐ yào bú yào chá? — Do you want tea (or not)?

quiz.q: The simplest way to form a yes/no question is:
options: move the verb to the front

quiz.q: Where does 什么 (what) go in a Mandarin question?

teaching.h: Aspect instead of tense — a genuinely different way of thinking about time
teaching.p: Rather than marking WHEN something happened, Mandarin marks HOW an action relates to time — is it done, ever-experienced, or ongoing right now? These three particles are the core toolkit.

teaching.h: 了 (le) — completion or a new state
teaching.p: Same particle from Lesson 3, now shown clearly marking a finished action.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ dào le — I've arrived

teaching.h: 过 (guo) — 'have you ever...'
teaching.p: Marks an experience that happened at least once, at some unspecified point, without saying exactly when — this is genuinely a different concept from just 'past tense'.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ qùguo Zhōngguó — I've been to China (at some point)

teaching.h: 在 (zài) — happening right now
teaching.p: Placed BEFORE the verb (unlike 了 and 过, which come after) to show an action currently in progress.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ zài chīfàn — I am eating

quiz.q: 我去___中国。(I've been to China)

teaching.h: Familiar categories, some surprising behavior
teaching.p: Mandarin has nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions — but a few of them behave in ways that'll surprise an English speaker.
teaching.exTranslation: to run, fast, teacher

teaching.h: 形容词 (adjectives) secretly act like verbs
teaching.p: This is the surprising part: Chinese adjectives function as stative verbs, meaning you DON'T need a 'to be' verb before them — 很高 already means 'is tall' on its own.
teaching.exTranslation: tā hěn gāo — She is tall. (no separate 'is' needed)

teaching.h: 副词 (adverbs) always come before the verb
teaching.p: Unlike English, which often puts adverbs after the verb ('runs quickly'), Mandarin puts them before ('quickly runs').
teaching.exTranslation: tā hěn kuài pǎo — He runs quickly. (literally: he quickly runs)

teaching.h: 介词 (preposition) phrases go before the verb too
teaching.p: Same 'before, not after' pattern — a whole prepositional phrase sits ahead of the verb, unlike English's 'eat at home'.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ zài jiā chīfàn — I eat at home. (literally: I at home eat)

quiz.q: In "她很高," what part of speech is "高"?

options: act like stative verbs, no 是 needed
quiz.answer: act like stative verbs, no 是 needed

quiz.q: 介词 phrases (like 在家) usually go:

teaching.h: 陈述句 — the plain statement
teaching.p: Just normal SVO order, nothing extra.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ xǐhuān māo — I like cats.

teaching.h: 疑问句 — the question
teaching.p: Formed with 吗, a question word, or A-not-A — all covered in Lesson 4.
teaching.exTranslation: nǐ xǐhuān māo ma? — Do you like cats?

teaching.h: 祈使句 — the command
teaching.p: 请 (please) softens a direct instruction and is genuinely important for sounding polite, not just correct.
teaching.exTranslation: qǐng zuò — Please sit.

teaching.h: 并列句 — the compound sentence
teaching.p: Connector words like 和 (and) and 但是 (but) link two ideas, similar to English.
teaching.ex: 我喜欢猫，但是我更喜欢狗。
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ xǐhuān māo, dànshì wǒ gèng xǐhuān gǒu — I like cats, but I like dogs more.

quiz.q: "请坐。" is an example of a:
请 (qǐng) is used to make a sentence:
A 并列句 joins two clauses using:

teaching.h: A concept with no real English equivalent
teaching.p: A complement is a word or phrase attached right after the verb that tells you the RESULT, DIRECTION, or DEGREE of the action. This is genuinely one of the more advanced, distinctive parts of Mandarin grammar.

teaching.h: Result complements — did it actually succeed?
teaching.p: 懂 (dǒng, 'understand') attached after 听 (tīng, 'listen') tells you the listening actually resulted in understanding — not just that listening happened.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ tīng dǒng le — I heard and understood.

teaching.h: Directional complements — which way?
teaching.p: 来 (come) or 去 (go) after a verb shows the direction of movement relative to the speaker.
teaching.exTranslation: tā zǒu jìnlái le — He walked in (toward the speaker).

teaching.h: Degree complements — how well?
teaching.p: 得 (de) plus an adjective after the verb describes the quality of how the action was done.
teaching.exTranslation: tā shuō de hěn hǎo — She speaks very well.

teaching.h: Potential complements — can or can't
teaching.p: Insert 得 (possible) or 不 (impossible) between the verb and complement to express ability.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ tīng de dǒng — I can understand. / wǒ tīng bù dǒng — I can't understand.

quiz.q: 得 + adjective after a verb is a:

teaching.h: 比 (bǐ) — the direct comparison word
teaching.p: Structure: A + 比 + B + adjective. Notice there's no separate word for 'than' — 比 itself carries that meaning.
teaching.exTranslation: tā bǐ wǒ gāo — He is taller than me.

teaching.h: 跟...一样 — expressing equality
teaching.p: Literally 'with...the same' — used when two things are equal in some way.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ gēn tā yíyàng gāo — I'm as tall as him.

teaching.h: 没有...那么 — expressing 'less than'
teaching.p: The negative counterpart to 比 — literally 'doesn't have...that much'.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ méiyǒu tā nàme gāo — I'm not as tall as him.

teaching.h: 最 (zuì) — the superlative
teaching.p: Simply placed before an adjective to mean 'the most'.
teaching.exTranslation: tā zuì gāo — He is the tallest.

options: He is as tall as me

teaching.h: 如果...就 — the most common if-then pattern
teaching.p: 如果 (if) sets up the condition, 就 (then) introduces the result — used for both realistic and hypothetical situations alike, since Mandarin doesn't grammatically distinguish them the way English/Spanish/German do.
teaching.exTranslation: rúguǒ xiàyǔ, wǒ jiù bú qù — If it rains, I won't go.

teaching.h: 要是...的话 — the conversational version
teaching.p: More common in casual spoken Mandarin than 如果.
teaching.ex: 要是你有时间的话，来吧。
teaching.exTranslation: yàoshi nǐ yǒu shíjiān dehuà, lái ba — If you have time, come.

teaching.h: No verb changes needed — genuinely simpler here
teaching.p: Unlike German/Spanish/English, which shift verb tense or mood for hypotheticals, Mandarin verbs stay exactly the same regardless — context and time words carry all the meaning.

teaching.h: 只要...就 — 'as long as'
teaching.p: Expresses a sufficient condition — do this one thing, and the result follows.
teaching.exTranslation: zhǐyào nǐ nǔlì, jiù huì chénggōng — As long as you try hard, you'll succeed.

options: a more conversational way to say "if"
quiz.answer: a more conversational way to say "if"

quiz.q: Do Mandarin conditional verbs change tense/form like in English?

teaching.h: 短语 — a chunk with no complete subject-verb pairing
teaching.exTranslation: at home, very happy

teaching.h: 从句 — has its own subject and verb
teaching.exTranslation: tā shuō de huà — what he said

teaching.h: 的-clauses turn a whole idea into a noun modifier
teaching.p: This is a distinctly Mandarin structure: 的 lets you attach an entire clause as a description before a noun, similar in function to English's relative clauses ('the book that I bought') but built completely differently.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ zuótiān mǎi de shū — the book I bought yesterday

teaching.h: Connector pairs link two clauses together
teaching.p: 因为...所以 (because...so) and 虽然...但是 (although...but) work as matched pairs, both halves appearing in the sentence — unlike English, which usually only needs one connector word.
teaching.exTranslation: yīnwèi xiàyǔ, suǒyǐ wǒ méi qù — Because it rained, so I didn't go.

quiz.q: "在家里" is an example of a:
我昨天买___书 (the book I bought — de)
的 turns a clause into a:

teaching.h: Two structures worth learning deliberately
teaching.p: These reorder the sentence in ways that feel unusual at first but are extremely common in real Mandarin — worth practicing beyond just recognizing them.

teaching.h: 把 (bǎ) — moving the object forward for emphasis
teaching.p: Pulls the object BEFORE the verb, emphasizing exactly what happened to it. Typically used when the action clearly disposes of, moves, or changes the object in a specific way.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ bǎ shū fàng zài zhuōzi shàng — I put the book on the table.

teaching.h: When 把 shows up in real usage
teaching.p: Especially common with specific, completed actions done TO something.
teaching.exTranslation: tā bǎ mén guān le — He closed the door.

teaching.h: 被 (bèi) — Mandarin's version of passive voice
teaching.p: Subject + 被 + (doer) + verb — the closest structural match to English's passive voice.
teaching.exTranslation: shū bèi tā ná zǒu le — The book was taken by him.

teaching.h: 被 works even without naming who did it
teaching.p: Just like English passive voice, you can drop the doer entirely if it's unknown or doesn't matter.
teaching.exTranslation: bēizi bèi dǎpò le — The cup was broken.

quiz.q: The 把 construction moves the object:
In a 被 sentence, can the doer be omitted?

teaching.h: Direct speech — the exact words
teaching.exTranslation: tā shuō: "wǒ hěn lèi." — He said, "I'm tired."

teaching.h: Indirect speech with 说 — genuinely simpler than English
teaching.p: Just 他说 (he said) plus the idea, no quotation marks needed.
teaching.exTranslation: tā shuō tā hěn lèi — He said he was tired.

teaching.h: No tense backshift required — a real relief for learners
teaching.p: Since Mandarin verbs don't change form for tense at all, there's nothing to shift when reporting speech — unlike the backshift rules in English, Spanish, and German.

teaching.h: Pronouns still shift to match the new speaker
teaching.p: 我 (I) in the original quote often becomes 他/她 (he/she) once someone else is reporting it.
teaching.exTranslation: "wǒ hěn máng" → tā shuō tā hěn máng — "I'm busy" → He said he was busy.

quiz.q: Does the verb change form in Mandarin reported speech?

options: quotation marks around the exact words

teaching.h: No capital letters at all
teaching.p: Chinese characters simply don't have an uppercase/lowercase distinction — every capitalization rule you've learned in other languages just doesn't apply here.

teaching.h: 、 vs. ， — two different commas with different jobs
teaching.p: 顿号 (、) separates items in a list specifically; the regular comma （，） is for pauses between clauses, similar to English's comma.
teaching.exTranslation: píngguǒ, xiāngjiāo, chéngzi — apples, bananas, oranges

teaching.h: Full-width punctuation looks visually different
teaching.p: Chinese punctuation marks (，。？！) are wider than their English counterparts — this is why Chinese text often looks visually distinct even before you read a single character.
teaching.exTranslation: nǐ hǎo ma? — How are you?

teaching.h: 《》 — marking titles, instead of italics or quotes
teaching.p: Where English might italicize a book title, Chinese wraps it in these angle-bracket-style marks.
teaching.exTranslation: wǒ zài dú "Hóng Lóu Mèng" — I'm reading Dream of the Red Chamber.

options: identical in width to English ones

teaching.h: Paired connectors — Mandarin's way of linking clauses
teaching.p: Unlike English's single connector words, Mandarin often uses matched PAIRS, one word in each clause, working together.
teaching.ex: 虽然很累，但是我很开心。
teaching.exTranslation: suīrán hěn lèi, dànshì wǒ hěn kāixīn — Although tired, I'm happy.

teaching.h: 因为...所以 — cause and result, both marked
teaching.p: Both 'because' and 'so' appear in the same sentence — this can feel redundant to an English speaker, but it's standard, expected Mandarin structure.
teaching.exTranslation: yīnwèi xiàyǔ, suǒyǐ wǒ méi qù — Because it rained, I didn't go.

teaching.h: 不但...而且 — stacking emphasis
teaching.p: Connects two escalating, related points — 'not only X, but also Y'.
teaching.exTranslation: tā búdàn cōngmíng, érqiě qínfèn — She's not only smart, but also hardworking.

teaching.h: 一边...一边 — two things happening at once
teaching.p: Describes simultaneous actions, both verbs marked with 一边.
teaching.ex: 他一边吃饭一边看电视。
teaching.exTranslation: tā yìbiān chīfàn yìbiān kàn diànshì — He eats while watching TV.

quiz.q: 不但...而且 is used to:
options: add emphasis to two related points
quiz.answer: add emphasis to two related points

teaching.h: 关联词 in more formal/written contexts
teaching.p: Similar function to English transitions, but these versions lean more formal — the ones from Lessons 7 and 15 (但是, 所以) are more casual equivalents you'd actually say out loud.
teaching.exTranslation: however, therefore, furthermore, for example

teaching.h: 然而 — formal contrast
teaching.ex: 他很努力。然而，他没有成功。
teaching.exTranslation: tā hěn nǔlì. rán'ér, tā méiyǒu chénggōng — He worked hard. However, he didn't succeed.

teaching.h: 因此 — formal cause/result
teaching.p: Common in writing more than casual speech.
teaching.ex: 下雨了，因此比赛取消了。
teaching.exTranslation: xiàyǔ le, yīncǐ bǐsài qǔxiāo le — It rained, therefore the match was cancelled.

teaching.h: 此外 — adding a further point
teaching.ex: 她很聪明，此外还很努力。
teaching.exTranslation: tā hěn cōngmíng, cǐwài hái hěn nǔlì — She's smart; furthermore, she's hardworking.
